lead: Both readings ask where true wisdom comes from. Paul tells the Corinthians, proud of their favourite teachers, that the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God, and that all things are theirs only because they belong to Christ. In John, Jesus says that those who are taught by God come to him, because he alone has seen the Father and is himself the bread of life. True wisdom is not something we own; it is Someone we receive.

set: The Corinthian church was divided into groups: “I belong to Paul”, “I belong to Apollos”, “I belong to Cephas” (1:12). Each group boasted of its leader as if he were a school of wisdom. Paul has shown that the cross looks like foolishness to the world (1:18–25), and that teachers are only servants and fellow workers in God’s field (3:5–9). Now he draws his conclusion.
str: v. 18: do not deceive yourselves; become a fool in order to become wise.
vv. 19–20: two proofs from Scripture: God catches the wise in their craftiness (Job 5:13); the Lord knows their thoughts are futile (Psalm 94:11).
vv. 21–23: do not boast in human leaders: all things are yours, you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s.
kw: Not learning as such, which Paul himself had. It is a way of thinking that measures everything by success, status and cleverness, and so cannot understand a crucified Messiah.
A favourite word of Paul in this letter. The only right boast is in the Lord (1:31, quoting Jeremiah 9:24).
The Corinthians wanted to belong to one teacher. Paul turns it round: the teachers belong to them, and so does the whole world, life, death, present and future, because they belong to Christ.
vv: If you think that you are wise in this age, you should become fools so that you may become wise.
Humility is the door of wisdom. Whoever thinks he already knows cannot be taught.
For the wisdom of this world is foolishness with God.
Paul reverses the Corinthians’ scale of values. What the world calls foolish, the cross, is God’s wisdom (1:24).
whether Paul or Apollos or Cephas or the world or life or death or the present or the future
A breathtaking list. Even death is “ours”, because in Christ it has become the way to life.
and you belong to Christ, and Christ belongs to God.
Christ “belongs to God” as the Son who receives everything from the Father and returns everything to him (15:28). The chain of belonging ends in the Father’s love.
ch: The Second Vatican Council closes its reflection on human activity spoiled by sin with these verses: all things are yours, and you are Christ’s, and Christ is God’s (Gaudium et Spes 37). The Christian does not despise the world or human wisdom; he receives them as gifts and orders them to Christ. St John Chrysostom, preaching on this passage, notes that Paul humbles the proud teachers by making them belong to their hearers, and lifts the hearers up by giving them all things (in substance, Homilies on 1 Corinthians).

set: Jesus is still speaking in the synagogue at Capernaum. He has said that no one can come to him unless the Father draws him (6:44). Now he explains how the Father draws: by teaching. He quotes the prophets and then repeats, more plainly, the claim that gave offence: “I am the bread of life.”
str: v. 45: it is written, “they shall all be taught by God”; whoever has learned from the Father comes to me.
v. 46: only the one who is from God has seen the Father.
v. 47: whoever believes has eternal life.
vv. 48–50: I am the bread of life; your ancestors ate manna and died; this bread is for not dying.
kw: Jesus is quoting Isaiah 54:13, a promise for the restored Jerusalem: “All your children shall be taught by the Lord.” Jeremiah too promised a covenant in which God himself would teach every heart (Jeremiah 31:34).

In John, Jesus often says “I am” with an image: bread, light, gate, shepherd, resurrection, way, vine. The words also echo the divine name revealed to Moses (Exodus 3:14), and sometimes stand alone (8:58).
The bread God gave Israel in the wilderness (Exodus 16). It was a true gift of God, but it fed bodily life only. Jesus does not despise it; he says it pointed beyond itself.
vv: It is written in the prophets, ‘And they shall all be taught by God.’ Everyone who has heard and learned from the Father comes to me.
The Father’s drawing is not blind force; it is teaching that the heart can hear and accept. Every true seeker of God is on the way to Christ.
Not that anyone has seen the Father except the one who is from God; he has seen the Father.
The Prologue said the same: “No one has ever seen God. It is God the only Son, who is close to the Father’s heart, who has made him known” (1:18).
Your ancestors ate the manna in the wilderness, and they died.
Jesus speaks to his own people of “your ancestors”, as Moses and the prophets did. The point is not blame but contrast: the manna sustained them for a time; the bread he gives sustains for ever.
ch: The Catechism teaches that Jesus, because he has seen the Father, is the only one who knows him and can reveal him (CCC 151, quoting 6:46), and that the Church sees in the manna in the desert a prefiguring of the Eucharist, the true bread from heaven (CCC 1094). St Augustine taught that Christ is the teacher within: human teachers speak to the ear, but it is Christ dwelling in the heart who teaches us to recognise the truth (in substance, The Teacher).

study: Paul says, “All things are yours… and you belong to Christ.” Which gifts in my life do I hold as if they were mine alone, rather than as gifts held in Christ?
Jesus says that all who are taught by God come to him. How do I let God teach me: in Scripture, in prayer, in the Church’s teaching, in the people he sends?
